source: Jiang et al. (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for Large Language Models - Table 4 (zero-shot ChatGPT; closes gap 10 for 2023)
finding: The real ChatGPT numbers. The Overall score is the mean of the Original, Semantic and Context accuracies, so the 53% and 63% in the text are the word and sentence overall scores. The two earlier evidence files agree once read this way (63 = sentence, 53 = word).
numbers: Sentence puzzles (627 items): Original 60.77, Semantic 59.33, Context 67.94, group Ori&Sem 50.72, group Ori&Sem&Con 39.71, overall 62.68. Word puzzles (492 items): Original 56.10, Semantic 52.44, Context 51.83, Ori&Sem 43.90, Ori&Sem&Con 29.27, overall 53.46. Human (102 sampled items): sentence overall 91.98 (90.74/90.74/94.44; group 88.89), word 91.67. Random: sentence 24.40, word 25.34. Best other models: RoBERTa-L sentence 43.38; FlanT5-11B word 39.84.
quote: models perform best on context reconstruction
limits: Model is 2023 ChatGPT, not a 2025 reasoning model. Human sample is 102 items. Multiple choice with a None-of-the-above option.
agent_relevance: Cite 62.68 (sentence) and 53.46 (word). Consistency across rewordings, not average accuracy, is the honest figure.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for Large Language Models - consistency drop and memorisation note
finding: Moving from single-item accuracy to solving the original plus both reworded versions cuts ChatGPT sharply. The authors say ChatGPT did best on original word puzzles and suspect memorisation of famous ones (for example COW in thirteen letters).
numbers: ChatGPT sentence: Original 60.77 to Ori&Sem&Con 39.71 (-21.1 pp). Word: 56.10 to 29.27 (-26.8 pp). Humans: sentence 90.74 to 88.89 (-1.9 pp), word 91.67 to 89.58 (-2.1 pp). The few-shot table (Table 8) came out garbled in text extraction and was not used.
limits: Gap 10 is only half closed: no 2025 reasoning-model consistency numbers were found (web search budget ran out). SemEval-2024 Task 9 systems report much higher sentence scores (one 0.975) under a different setup.
agent_relevance: Score the scaffold on the consistency metric (original plus two rewordings), where the model has most to lose and the scaffold most to show.

source: Ormerod & MacGregor (2020) The complementary roles of knowledge and strategy in insight problem-solving - Experiment 1 (full text)
finding: Chunk tightness matters (as RCT predicts), but a large number disparity almost erases it (as progress monitoring predicts). Both main effects were significant; the interaction was not.
numbers: N=121 analysed of 129 recruited; Roman-numeral matchsticks, 5 min, between subjects. Solved: low-value loose 23/30 (77%), low-value tight 13/30 (43%; the table prints 11/29, 40%), high-value loose 28/31 (90%), high-value tight 24/31 (77%). Logistic model chi2(3)=21.6, p=.001; Chunking Wald 8.12 p=.004; Value Wald 8.65 p=.003; interaction n.s. First moves on loose chunks: low-value 28/30 (93%) and 22/29 (76%); high-value 21/31 (63%) and 16/31 (52%). First-move model: Value Wald 8.86 p=.003, Chunking Wald 4.71 p=.030.
limits: One item per cell, and the two tight-chunk items differ (operator + vs numeral [). Between subjects, 5 min, one lab family. Text and table disagree slightly on cell counts; both are reported.
agent_relevance: These are the 12% and 62% figures behind claim K06 (verified from the full text). Any LLM test of O4 should hold number disparity fixed, or it will confuse constraint relaxation with an arithmetic-gap cue.

finding: The hardest Knoblich class (standard tautology) is hard mainly when no number gives a cue. With a large value gap it was solved nearly as often as the easy reverse tautology. Reverse tautologies (constraint removed from the statement) were easy either way.
numbers: N=133 analysed of 144. Standard tautology: low value 4/32 (12%), high value 21/34 (62%). Reverse tautology: low 23/32 (72%), high 28/35 (77%). Logistic model chi2(3)=39.30, p<.001; Tautology Wald 19.33 p<.001; Value Wald 11.12 p=.001; interaction Wald 5.26 p=.022.
limits: One item per cell. The authors' reading, that relaxation is unnecessary, is an interpretation, not a model test.
agent_relevance: The order value < operator < tautology holds in humans only when value cues are held low. For gap 2, fix the number gap or the LLM order will be confounded.

source: Ormerod & MacGregor (2020) - discussion; Jones (2003); no implemented RCT model (gaps 5, 6, 7)
finding: The authors argue solvers succeeded because moves that reduce the disparity happened to lie on the solution path, not because knowledge was suspended. They cite Jones 2003, Ormerod et al 2002 and 2013, and Nakano 2017 as other support for progress monitoring, and point to Ohlsson 2011 for only a partial specification of an RCT model.
numbers: No new numbers beyond d03 and d04. They say CSPT cannot explain the initial difficulty of matchsticks; that is left to RCT.
quote: an account which has no need for relaxation of prior knowledge to discover solutions will benefit from greater parsimony
limits: Jones 2003 itself was not opened (paywalled). The comparison is human only: no study separates monitoring from restructuring in LLM traces.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open for LLMs. A head-to-head would score each trace for (a) a switched move after a stall and (b) a changed representation, then regress the outcome on both. In humans neither theory is ruled out.

source: d'Aliberti & Horta Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models (arXiv 2601.00514 v2) - Table 5 forced reconsideration (gap 4)
finding: Appending a reconsideration cue to a second generation raises math accuracy a lot, crosswords a little, Rush Hour not at all. Pass 2 is a fresh generation at the same decoding settings plus the cue, compared with Pass 1.
numbers: Mostly Qwen2.5-1.5B GRPO checkpoints (also Qwen 7B, Llama 8B). Math: N=320,000 paired, 32.21% to 40.62% (+8.41 pp), wins 50,574 vs losses 23,500. Crosswords: N=83,200, 9.70% to 10.15% (+0.45 pp), wins 5,380 vs losses 5,004. Rush Hour 0.0233% to 0.0363% (+0.01 pp). Appendix table (math N=464,000): 32.70 to 40.43 (+7.74).
limits: No arm of a second generation without the cue. Pass 2 costs about twice the tokens. Small models. Fixed cue text, though three other wordings gave the same direction.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open for equal-token comparison. A plain independent resample has the same mean accuracy as Pass 1, so the +8.41 pp is more than 'two tries' on the mean, but best-of-2 or majority at 2x tokens was never run.

source: d'Aliberti & Horta Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models (arXiv 2601.00514 v2) - entropy buckets, cue wording, external models
finding: The gain is concentrated where Pass-1 entropy was high. Three cue wordings (C1 to C3) all helped; one standard deviation more entropy raised the odds of a correct Pass 2 by 2.2 to 2.5 times. DeepSeek-R1 and GPT-4o also show shifts in only a few percent of traces, and shifted traces are not more accurate.
numbers: Table 29 (count-weighted): overall 18.04 to 22.11 (+4.07); high-entropy 11.18 to 19.27 (+8.09); low-entropy 19.75 to 22.82 (+3.07). Math high 19.70 to 35.09 (+15.38), math low 35.94 to 41.77 (+5.82). Crosswords high +1.04, low +0.36. Spontaneous shifts in math: raw -7.40 pp (high entropy), -22.88 pp (low entropy). External models: math shift rates DeepSeek-R1 0.96 to 1.83%, GPT-4o 2.98 to 7.31%; GPT-4o MATH-500 T=0.3 shifted 63.2% vs non-shifted 64.9%.
limits: My inference, not the authors': buckets are chosen on Pass-1 entropy and Pass-1 accuracy in the high bucket is low (19.7%). A plain resample of the same items would regress toward the item mean and also rise, so the +15.38 is partly selection. The overall +8.41 is not affected.
agent_relevance: If the scaffold gates a reconsideration step on uncertainty, compare it with a gated plain resample, not an ungated baseline.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025-2026) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles Reveal Fundamental Limits of Machine Insight (NazoNazo; arXiv 2509.14704 v3) - Table 2 verification failure (gap 3)
finding: Re-opened. The 5.23% to 39.34% figures appear only in version 3; versions 1 and 2 call the thought-log analysis qualitative. Share of wrong answers where a gold-answer string appears in the thought log before the final line.
numbers: Answered / correct / verification failures: DeepSeek-R1-0528 199/42/48 = 30.57% of wrong; Gemini 2.5 Flash Preview 201/29/9 = 5.23%; Claude Opus 4 201/61/35 = 25.00%; Grok 4 194/72/48 = 39.34%. Ceiling if every failure were recovered (my arithmetic): DeepSeek 21% to 45%; Gemini 14% to 19%; Claude 30% to 48%; Grok 37% to 62% correct.
limits: Literal string match counts any appearance of the answer word, including in rejected or incidental text, and the table accuracies differ from the paper's main scoring. Four models. Not preregistered, no inter-rater agreement. Humans rarely fail this way, per the authors.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly closed: verification failures are real and large, but the ceiling for a harvest-and-commit step is an upper bound, and the commit rule still has to pick the right candidate among many. Needs an A/B on logged traces: commit last vs most repeated vs verifier-chosen.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025-2026) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles Reveal Fundamental Limits of Machine Insight (NazoNazo; arXiv 2509.14704 v3) - human and model accuracy, GPT-5, contamination (gap 9)
finding: Update to K10: most models are far below humans, but GPT-5 fell inside the human 95% interval. Reasoning models beat non-reasoning models. Retrieval-free scores were low, which the authors take as limited contamination; items sit on a public website.
numbers: 201 riddles; human reference n=126 on a 120-item subset, mean 52.9% (95% CI 46.6 to 59.2). 38 models, zero-shot, no retrieval. Non-reasoning mean 7.6%, reasoning mean 17.6% on the 120 subset. Reasoning vs non-reasoning, 201 items: odds ratio 2.29 (95% CI 1.99 to 2.64). Cohen's d 0.946 in the earlier version. Size did not predict accuracy; release date did. Planned split: 42 open items, 159 blind (including the 120).
limits: GPT-5 overlap with the human CI is descriptive, with no formal test. Contamination is argued, not measured.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly closed for riddles, not for classic insight problems. Use blind NazoNazo-style items, or freshly generated Roman-numeral matchsticks, for any scaffold test.

source: MathSticks authors (2025) MathSticks: A Benchmark for Visual Symbolic Compositional Reasoning with Matchstick Puzzles (Tables 4, 5)
finding: Seven-segment matchstick benchmark. Sign-changed puzzles are harder for o3 in both regimes. Text input helps a lot.
numbers: o3 with text: 1-move 82.50, 2-move 52.88; sign-changed 51.45 vs unchanged 65.19. Without text: 1-move 70.00, 2-move 32.12; sign-changed 34.20 vs 41.22. Overall o3 60.00 with text, 38.50 without; Gemini-2.5-Pro 45.25 and Flash 26.50 (text); GPT-4o 0.00; humans 91.72 (3 people). Open-source models 0.00.
limits: Row labels in the extracted tables are shifted by one line; I gave the first row to o3 because it matches the 60.00 headline, and other rows may be mislabeled. No chunk manipulation (seven-segment digits), no trace analysis, no scaffold arm.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2 stay open. The generator is public and enumerates legal moves, so it could be adapted to Roman numerals with tagged constraint types.

source: Kershaw (2004) Key Actions in Insight Problems: Further Evidence for the Importance of Non-Dot Turns in the Nine-Dot Problem (CogSci 26)
finding: Non-dot turns, not drawing outside the dots, predict nine-dot solution. Training that removes the hidden constraints gave about 40% solving; the classic unaided rate is about 0%.
numbers: Unaided nine-dot typically 0% (MacGregor et al 2001, as cited). MacGregor variants: 88% after four attempts with no non-dot turn vs 27% with one. Kershaw & Ohlsson (2004) with training: 11-dot 97%, 10-dot 80%, displaced nine-dot 50%, nine-dot 40%, three-turn 30%. This paper, Exp 1 (N=150 trained, first line given, 4 min): 83%, 60%, 38%, 40%, 50%; none differs from the earlier data (all p>.05). 83% (99/120) drew lines outside the dots. Weisberg & Alba (1981): first line plus 'go outside the box' gave 62%.
limits: About 30 people per problem. MacGregor and Weisberg & Alba figures are second-hand here. This corrects the earlier note: the unaided baseline is about 0% by this source, and the 37% control in Kershaw & Ohlsson 2001 is a different group.
agent_relevance: Difficulty has several causes, so one reframing operator will not fix every impasse. Hints that remove only one cause help little.

source: Oellinger et al. (2014) The dynamics of search, impasse and representational change provide a coherent explanation of difficulty in the nine-dot problem (Psychological Research)
finding: Three incremental hint conditions (a route, plus the meeting dot, plus non-dot points) gave faster representational change and more solutions than a control. The paper proposes a model of heuristics plus representational change.
numbers: No numbers: the Springer page is paywalled and only the abstract and reference list were read.
limits: Abstract only. The gap-6 question about full Oellinger 2006 and 2013 numbers is not closed.
agent_relevance: Supports staged hinting: tell the agent which dimension to re-open.

source: Oellinger, Jones, Knoblich (2006) Heuristics and representational change in two-move matchstick arithmetic tasks (Advances in Cognitive Psychology 2(4), 239-253)
finding: Abstract-level only: representational change required had a strong effect on solution rates while heuristics had a minimal effect; the model makes representational change a precondition for heuristics to apply.
numbers: N=120, two problem types. No cell numbers obtained; the full text (core.ac.uk, ac-psych.org, NTU repository) returned a Cloudflare block.
limits: Not opened, hence opened:false. Gap 6 stays open for this paper.
agent_relevance: Do not treat 'heuristics have minimal effect' as established until the full text is read.

source: Ohlsson (1992) Information-processing explanations of insight and related phenomena; Ohlsson (2011) Deep Learning
finding: Secondary descriptions only: impasse, then one of three processes (elaboration, re-encoding, constraint relaxation) drives representational change; the model also includes search before impasse.
numbers: No numbers: the chapter and the 2011 book are not online. Gap 6 stays open for Ohlsson.
agent_relevance: The three-way split maps to O6 (re-encode), O4 (relax), and an 'elaborate' step that adds knowledge. Our schema has no explicit elaborate operator.

source: Gap search note: LLM, matchstick and constraint-relaxation studies (gaps 1, 2, 7, 8)
finding: Searches before the web budget ran out found no study testing an explicit constraint-listing and relax step against sampling or best-of-k on matchsticks, none testing Knoblich's order in LLMs, no executable RCT simulator, and no typed-memory test for agents. The only matchstick LLM paper found was MathSticks.
numbers: Zero direct hits. The 200-call web search budget ran out mid-run; the arXiv search page, the arXiv API and OpenAlex returned 429 or empty.
limits: Absence of evidence from a limited search, not proof. Frontiers 2025 (c27) and Nasvytis 2026 were not re-opened.
agent_relevance: These four gaps are experiments to run, not facts to cite.
